Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 322 Aerial Ungulate Survey for Moose 
(2018) 
 
Background 
An aerial ungulate survey for moose was conducted in December 2018 in Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 322 
using transect survey methodology. This WMU is located in the Lower Foothills Natural Region of west central 
Alberta and is 1,435 km2. Prior to 2018, WMU 322 was surveyed in 1999, 2000, 2002 and 2012 using a random 
stratified block methodology. It was also previously flown in 2015 using transect survey methodology. Previous 
population estimates for moose are provided in Table 1. The population and density estimates were determined as 
a proportion of the total survey based on WMU area.  
 
During the 2018 aerial survey, sightings of white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were recorded and population 
estimates were completed for these three species as well using transect survey methodology. Population 
estimates for white-tailed deer and mule deer were calculated previously for WMU 322 during the 1999, 2002, 
2012 and 2015 aerial surveys, however no previous population estimates for elk were completed. Previous year’s 
population and density estimates for white-tailed deer are provided in Table 2 and population and density 
estimates for mule deer are provided in Table 3. All of these above observations were recorded and entered into 
the Fisheries and Wildlife Management Information System (FWMIS) at the completion of the survey. 
 
In WMU 322, the antlered and antlerless moose archery only season runs from September 1 to October 31 and the 
general (rifle) season runs from November 1 to 30. Both the archery only and the general (rifle) require Special 
Licences obtained through the Special Licence application process.  
  
Hunter harvest data in WMU 322 for moose Special Licences indicate five-year (2014 to 2018) average success as 
follows: antlered moose 82% and antlerless moose 83%. Over the past five-years on average; 29 Antlered Moose 
Special Licences were issued annually and 16 Antlerless Moose Special Licences annually were issued.  
 
The primary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose populations in WMU 322 by determining 
a population estimate based on density estimates, and a population demographic split for sex and age classes.  
The secondary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of white -tailed deer, mule deer and elk 
populations in WMU 322 by determining a population estimate based on density estimates, and a popu lation 
demographic split for sex and age classes. 
 
Survey Method 
 
The transect survey was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) intervals, with 25% coverage (400 
metre wide survey strip) requiring a total of 9.5 hours of flight time to complete the survey. Surveying was 
completed on the following dates in December; 
 
 December 7 (5.7 flight hours) 
 December 8 (0.5 flight hours) 
 December 9 (3.0 flight hours) 
 
At each observation point, we counted moose and we determined sex and age and verified that each observation 
was within the transect width. For white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk we classified each observation for sex and 
age class, but did not record antler size.   
 
Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average densit y (R; #/km2) of 
moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (∑x) by total area searched (length of transects

multiplied by 400 metre survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without 
replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). No correction factor was 
applied for moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N -n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as  the 
number of transects sampled. 
 
Results 
 
For WMU 322 we surveyed 26 transects out of a possible 104 on December 7 to 9, 2018 for a total survey effort of 
900 km of transects and a survey area of 360 km 2 (25.09 % of WMU). In total, we counted 223 moose from 90 
groups. Of the 223 moose that were classified, 42 (19%) were bulls, 105 (47%) were cows, and 76 (34%) were 
calves. The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.40 and 0.72, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.62/km 2 
with a 90% confidence interval of 0.50/km2 to 0.74 km2. This corresponds to a 90% confidence interval that is +/- 
19% of the density estimate. The estimated moose abundance is 889 (718, 1060). We estimated the 2018 post -
hunting season winter moose population split to be 169 bulls, 418 cows, an d 302 calves. The 2018 moose survey 
results and previous survey population and density estimates for moose are provided in Table 1.  
 
Table 1. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for moose in WMU 322. Survey types have 
included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods. 
Year Survey Type Population Estimate Moose/km2 +/-% bull:cow:calf 
1999 RSB 724 0.54 22.8 26:100:53 
2002 RSB 548 0.38 26.5 75:100:68 
2012 RSB 504 0.35 20.4 69:100:64 
2015 Transect 458 0.32 10.5 67:100:87 
2018 Transect  889 0.62 19.0 40:100:72 
 
Survey effort parameters for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were identical to what was surveyed for moose 
and outlined above. Population estimates were calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk using the same 
methodology as outlined for moose (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969) for transects of varying lengths.  
  
A total of 374 white-tailed deer were observed in 108 groups, of which 357 were classified. Of the white-tailed deer 
classified there were 33 (9%) bucks, 210 (59%) does and 114 (32%) fawns. The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios 
were .15 and .56 respectively. The final density estimate for white-tailed deer was 1.04 /km2 for a final post-hunting 
season winter estimate of 1,491 white-tailed deer. We estimated the post-hunting season winter population split to 
be 134 bucks, 880 does and 477 fawns.

A total of 63 mule deer were observed in six groups. Of the mule deer classified observed there were 10 (16%) 
bucks, 34 (54%) does and 19 (30%) fawns. The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were .29 and .56 respectively. The 
final density estimate for mule deer was 0.17 /km2 for a final post-hunting season winter estimate of 251 mule deer.    
 
We estimated the post-hunting season winter population split to be 40 bucks, 135 does and 75 fawns. The 
population estimate should be used cautiously due to the low number and groups of mule deer observed during 
the survey.   
 
Table 3. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for mule deer in WMU 322. Survey types have 
included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods.  
Year Survey Type Population Estimate MUDE/km2 buck:doe:fawn 
1999 RSB 1,000 0.69 NA

2015 Transect 249 0.17 52:100:96 
2018 Transect  251 0.17 29:100:56 
 
A total of 57 elk were observed in two groups. Due to the low number of groups (2) of elk which were observed it is 
problematic to provide a statistically reliable population estimate for elk. Based on surveying 25% of the WMU, and 
observing 57 elk, a simplistic density estimate 0.16 elk/km2 equates to a population estimate of 227 elk.  
 
Of the 57 elk observed there were 3 bull, 41 cows and 13 calves classified. There has been no previous population 
estimate for elk in WMU 322 during any of the previous aerial surveys.
